lesson.subject: maths
lesson.title: Big Numbers
lesson.summary: Place value to 10,000, rounding, adding and taking away big numbers, negative numbers, Roman numerals and sequences.
learning_objectives: Read, write and order numbers to 10,000
Round, add and take away big numbers
Use negative numbers and Roman numerals

standards.text: Recognise the place value of each digit in a four-digit number; round to the nearest 10, 100 or 1,000
Add and subtract numbers with up to four digits using columns

success_criteria: I can say what each digit in a number to 10,000 is worth
I can add and take away 4-digit numbers
I can find a rule in a number sequence
lesson.real_life: Reading the height of mountains, the price of things in rupees and pounds, and the temperature on a winter day.

warm_up.prompt: The 5 in 5,000 is worth five thousand.
warm_up.explanation: The 5 is in the thousands place.

blocks.markdown: Today's big question: how do we read, write and compare really big numbers, like the height of K2 (8,611 m)?
blocks.say: Welcome, number explorer! K2, the second highest mountain in the world, is in Pakistan. It is eight thousand, six hundred and eleven metres high. How do we read, write and compare numbers that big? Today you will become a big number expert. You will read numbers up to ten thousand, round them, add and take away, explore negative numbers, and spot patterns. Let's climb!

blocks.alt: K2 in Pakistan is 8,611 metres high.
blocks.caption: K2 in Pakistan is 8,611 metres high.

blocks.text: Stop 1: Thousands, hundreds, tens and ones

blocks.markdown:
A number up to 9,999 has four places: **thousands**, **hundreds**, **tens** and **ones**.

Each place is ten times bigger than the one on its right.
blocks.say: Big numbers are not scary. They are built from four little parts, called places. From the right they are ones, tens, hundreds and thousands. Let's build the number four thousand, three hundred and seventy-two, one place at a time. Watch how the number grows.

scenes.caption: 4 thousands = 4,000
scenes.say: Start on the left with the thousands. There are four thousands. That is four thousand.

scenes.caption: 3 hundreds = 300
scenes.say: Next, the hundreds. Three hundreds make three hundred.

scenes.caption: 7 tens = 70 and 2 ones = 2
scenes.say: Then seven tens, which is seventy, and two ones, which is two.
Put them all together and we get four thousand, three hundred and seventy-two. We write it 4,372, with a comma after the thousands.

question.prompt: In the number 2,764, what does the 7 stand for?
question.explanation: The 7 is in the hundreds place, so it is worth 700.

blocks.markdown:
To add 1,000 only the thousands digit changes: 3,250 becomes 4,250.

10 more changes the tens digit and 100 more changes the hundreds digit.
blocks.say: Here is a super power. To make a number ten more, only the tens digit changes. For one hundred more, only the hundreds digit changes. For one thousand more, only the thousands digit changes. The other digits stay still. Try with three thousand, two hundred and fifty. One thousand more is four thousand, two hundred and fifty.

blocks.alt: 10 more, 100 more or 1,000 more changes one digit only.
blocks.caption: 10 more, 100 more or 1,000 more changes one digit only.

blocks.markdown:
To **round** to the nearest 100, look at the tens digit. 5 or more rounds up. 4 or less rounds down.

372 is closer to 400, so it rounds to 400.
blocks.say: Rounding gives us a friendly number that is close. To round to the nearest hundred, look at the tens digit. Four or less, stay where you are. Five or more, go up to the next hundred. Look at three hundred and seventy-two on the number line. It sits between three hundred and four hundred. It is closer to four hundred, so it rounds up to four hundred.

blocks.title: 372 on the line from 300 to 400
blocks.caption: 372 is past the halfway mark of 350, so it rounds up to 400.

question.explanation: The tens digit 8 is 5 or more, so round up to 5,400.

points: Four places: thousands, hundreds, tens, ones
Round: 5 or more goes up, 4 or less stays
blocks.say: Remember. Each place is ten times bigger than the place on its right. To round, look at the digit just to the right of the place you are rounding to.

terms.meaning: Big groups of one thousand. In 4,372 there are 4 thousands.
Groups of one hundred. In 4,372 there are 3 hundreds.
To change a number to a close, easier one, such as the nearest 100.

sub_lessons.title: Adding and taking away big numbers

blocks.markdown:
Write numbers in columns. Start with the **ones** and **carry** when a column makes ten or more.

Add 2,468 + 1,357 one column at a time.
blocks.say: To add big numbers, line them up in columns, ones under ones, tens under tens. Always start with the ones on the right. Let's add two thousand, four hundred and sixty-eight, and one thousand, three hundred and fifty-seven. Eight and seven make fifteen. We write five and carry one ten across.

scenes.caption: 8 + 7 = 15. Write 5, carry 1.
scenes.say: Ones first. Eight plus seven is fifteen. Write five, and carry one ten to the tens column.

scenes.caption: 6 + 5 + 1 = 12. Write 2, carry 1.
scenes.say: Tens next. Six plus five plus the carried one makes twelve. Write two, and carry one hundred.

scenes.caption: 4 + 3 + 1 = 8, then 2 + 1 = 3.
scenes.say: Hundreds. Four plus three plus one is eight. Then thousands. Two plus one is three.
The answer is three thousand, eight hundred and twenty-five.

blocks.title: Trade hundreds for a thousand
blocks.goal: Each block is 100. Drag 10 blocks into the Thousands box to make 1,000.
blocks.say: Here are twenty blocks. Each block is one hundred. Drag ten of them into the Thousands box. Ten hundreds make one thousand! That trade is exactly what carrying means.

blocks.markdown:
When you cannot take away, **exchange**: swap one from the next place left for ten here.

Check with the opposite: 2,387 + 2,817 should make 5,204.
blocks.say: Taking away works the same way, but we exchange instead of carry. Look at five thousand, two hundred and four, take away two thousand, eight hundred and seventeen. We cannot take seven from four. So we swap one ten for ten ones. When a place has nothing to swap, we go to the next place left. Finally, always check with the opposite sum. Add your answer back and you should get the number you started with.

blocks.alt: Subtract, then check by adding the answer back.
blocks.caption: Subtract, then check by adding the answer back.

question.hint: Exchange from the hundreds, then the tens.

blocks.title: Shop receipt maths
materials: A real shopping receipt or a price list
instructions: Pick two prices from the receipt that are in rupees or pounds and are over 1,000 pence or rupees.
Take the smaller from the bigger in columns.
Check each answer using the opposite sum.
blocks.say: Time to try it away from the screen. Use a pencil and paper and a few real prices.

blocks.answer_markdown: Yes! Ten thousands make ten thousand. That is the next place to the left after the thousands.

points: Line up columns and start with the ones
Carry when a column makes ten or more
Exchange when you cannot take away, then check with the opposite sum
blocks.say: Remember. Add and take away in columns, starting from the ones. Carry when a column makes ten or more, and exchange when you cannot take away. Always check with the opposite sum.

terms.meaning: Moving ten from one column into the next column to the left.
Swapping one from the next place for ten in this place when taking away.
Numbers lined up, ones under ones, tens under tens.
Adding to check a take away, or taking away to check an add.

blocks.markdown:
**Negative numbers** are below zero. −3 is colder than 0.

The further below zero, the smaller the number.
blocks.say: Have you ever seen a temperature of minus three? Numbers below zero are called negative numbers. On a thermometer, zero is freezing, and the numbers keep going down below zero. Watch the mercury drop from five degrees, past zero, to minus three.

scenes.caption: 5°C
scenes.say: It is five degrees. That is a cool day in Murree.

scenes.caption: 0°C
scenes.say: The temperature falls to zero. Water would freeze now.

scenes.caption: −3°C
scenes.say: It keeps falling to minus three. That is three degrees below zero. Minus three is smaller than zero.

question.hint: The further below zero, the colder.

blocks.markdown:
**Roman numerals** use letters: I = 1, V = 5, X = 10, L = 50, C = 100.

A smaller letter before a bigger one is taken away: IV = 4. After it, we add: VI = 6.
blocks.say: Long ago, Romans wrote numbers using letters. I is one, V is five, X is ten, L is fifty and C is one hundred. When a smaller letter comes before a bigger one, you take it away. IV is four, which is five take away one. When it comes after, you add. VI is six. You can still see Roman numerals on clock faces.

blocks.title: Roman numerals
blocks.caption: The five Roman letters we use.

points: Roman numerals use letters: IV = 4, VI = 6
blocks.say: Remember. Negative numbers are below zero, and the further below zero the smaller they are. Roman numerals use letters, and a smaller letter before a bigger one is taken away.

The number between the positive and negative numbers.

blocks.markdown:
K2 is 8,611 m high. Ben Nevis is 1,345 m high.

To find **the difference**, take the smaller number away from the bigger one.
blocks.say: Big numbers help us compare real things. K2 in Pakistan is the second highest mountain in the world. It is eight thousand, six hundred and eleven metres high. Ben Nevis in Scotland is the highest mountain in the United Kingdom. It is one thousand, three hundred and forty-five metres high. To find out how much higher K2 is, we take away.

scenes.caption: K2: 8,611 m
scenes.say: Here is K2. It is 8,611 metres high.

scenes.caption: Ben Nevis: 1,345 m
scenes.say: Here is Ben Nevis. It is 1,345 metres high. It is much smaller.

scenes.caption: 8,611 − 1,345 = 7,266 m
scenes.say: The difference is eight thousand, six hundred and eleven take away one thousand, three hundred and forty-five. That is seven thousand, two hundred and sixty-six metres.

question.prompt: A tower is 3,200 m high. A hill is 1,150 m high. How many metres higher is the tower?
question.hint: Take the smaller from the bigger.

blocks.markdown:
A **sequence** follows a rule. 3,000, 3,500, 4,000, 4,500 ... the rule is add 500.

Find the rule, then keep going.
blocks.say: A sequence is a list of numbers that follows a rule. Look at three thousand, three thousand five hundred, four thousand, four thousand five hundred. The rule is add five hundred each time. Once you spot the rule, you can find any number that comes next.

scenes.say: Add five hundred. That is three thousand five hundred.
Add five hundred again. Four thousand. And again, four thousand five hundred.

question.hint: Work out how much it goes up each time.

blocks.title: Number detective
materials: A book about mountains or an atlas
instructions: Find three tall mountains or buildings and write their heights.
Put them in order from tallest to shortest.
Work out the difference between the tallest and the shortest.
Write a sequence of your own and ask someone to find the rule.
blocks.say: Now be a number detective with a real list of heights or prices.

points: The difference: bigger take away smaller
Find the rule, then continue the pattern
blocks.say: Remember. The difference is the bigger number take away the smaller. A sequence follows a rule, so find the rule first.

terms.meaning: How much bigger one number is than another. Found by taking away.
A list of numbers that follows a rule.
What changes each time, like add 500.
A unit of length. A door is about 2 metres high.
